Music theory

Understand the neck. Play what you see.

Pick one idea, look at its diagram, then try it on your instrument. Each lesson gives you a short exercise and something concrete to listen for.

Try it on the fretboard ↗

Choose a lesson

Fretboard notes ↗

A fret is one semitone. The same note appears in several places: use the open strings and the 12th fret as landmarks.

Pentatonic ↗

A minor pentatonic uses A C D E G. Learn a small area first, then turn it into a phrase.

Triads ↗

A triad contains a root, a third and a fifth. The three shapes below contain the same A minor notes: A C E.

Chords ↗

Choose a root to see all its chords. Compare open, barre and compact shapes, then use a position that suits the song and your hand.

Daily routine ↗

Keep A minor as your reference and connect notes, pentatonic phrases, triads and rhythm.

Reading tablature ↗

Lines tell you the strings, numbers tell you the frets, and rhythm tells you when. Read two short examples, then decode the common technique symbols.

Understand

Start with the open strings, then find A. Use that same note as the root of a scale, a triad and a chord. The diagrams link these ideas without asking you to memorise the whole neck.

Standard tuning: E A D G B E, from the thickest string to the thinnest.

Make the connection

Choose a starting point from what you want to play: accompaniment needs chord changes and pulse; a melody needs string, fret and rhythm; improvising connects a scale to chord tones. You can work on one of these without finishing every theory lesson. Tune first so that a misplaced finger and an out-of-tune string are not confused.

Play it

Spend two minutes on a single diagram. Play slowly, look away, and repeat from memory. Return to the diagram only to check.

The two bars use A, C and E, then reverse the order. They belong to A minor. First locate each string and fret without a clock, then play one note per click. This links the map, the triad and a musical phrase in one small exercise.

Six lines, from top to bottom: e B G D A E. String 1 is the thin E. The examples use standard tuning without a capo. Move the hand when needed instead of forcing a wide stretch.

A worked example

Read left to right. Counts above mark the beats; numbers on the lines are frets; numbers below give the duration in beats. R = rest. Stacked fret numbers sound together. Start at 60 BPM.

Read the example as text
  1. Bar 1
    1. String 5 (A), Fret 0, A · 1 beats
    2. String 5 (A), Fret 3, C · 1 beats
    3. String 4 (D), Fret 2, E · 1 beats
    4. String 3 (G), Fret 2, A · 1 beats
  2. Bar 2
    1. String 3 (G), Fret 2, A · 1 beats
    2. String 4 (D), Fret 2, E · 1 beats
    3. String 5 (A), Fret 3, C · 1 beats
    4. String 5 (A), Fret 0, A · 1 beats

A mistake to avoid

Collecting shapes without naming or listening to their notes makes it difficult to reuse them. Change only one thing at a time: note, rhythm or position.

Listen and check

The notes use international names: A B C D E F G. A sharp (♯) raises a note by one fret; a flat (♭) lowers it by one fret. A♯ and B♭ sound the same in this tuning.

Ready for the next step?

Play both bars twice at a steady pulse, then find A somewhere else. If you lose the count, repeat one bar before adding the second.
